topic: Why the world's busiest shipping shortcut is running out of water
rights_notes: Checked against the three revenue-destroying categories and the two hard blocks, one at a time. (1) Music: no existing song, cover, remix or mashup is involved; the score will be original AI-generated audio, so no Content ID claim routes the revenue away. (2) Film/TV recreation: nothing is re-enacted. The format's shot vocabulary is chart, map, comparison and host_bumper, all built from raw numbers, so there is no underlying audiovisual work to infringe and no reused-content exposure. (3) COPPA: the subject is freight economics, auction clearing prices and hydrology for an adult general audience; the episode will be set 'not made for kids', keeping personalised ads, comments and end screens. Hard block A, screen recordings of software this machine does not run: none needed, every visual is generated. Hard block B, a living private individual as central figure: the central figure is a waterway and a state agency, the Panama Canal Authority; the only named humans would be public officials acting in office, and none is required for the episode to work. Two residual risks that are real but manageable, not blocking. First, stock footage: the widely circulated canal footage belongs to Reuters, CNBC, BBC and the ACP press office, and using it invites both Content ID and the reused-content rule, so the episode uses only NASA Earth Observatory imagery (public domain) and Copernicus Sentinel imagery (CC BY-SA, credited on screen) plus original renders. Second, charts: ACP transit and draft figures are uncopyrightable facts, but ACP's own chart images are not, so every chart is rebuilt from the raw series. Trademark: the canal is referred to descriptively; no ACP logo appears. Nothing here is a demonetising controversial-issues topic, since the episode reports hydrology and prices rather than arguing climate politics.
angle: Every incumbent has made the same video: the lake is low, ships are queuing, here is the $1.6bn fix. This episode makes the canal a water market instead of a drought story. A Panamax transit flushes about 52 million gallons of Gatun Lake into the sea, roughly 197,000 cubic metres, and that lake is also the drinking water for more than half of Panama. So when a shipping line pays $5.3 million at a slot auction to jump the queue, it has put a price on that water: divide the bid by the water the transit spends and the implied cost lands near $27 per cubic metre, against the roughly $0.26 per cubic metre a Panama City household was billed. That single ratio, charted across the auction record from the $135,000 baseline through the 2023 drought spike to the 2026 highs, is the spine of the episode: the canal does not sell passage, it sells fresh water, and the price it can charge tells you exactly how scarce that water has become. It also reframes Rio Indio, which reads as an infrastructure project in every competitor video and reads here as a state buying back its own water supply for $1.6 billion because the auction proved what the water was worth. No competitor has priced the water; they have all described the queue.
affiliate_angle: A monthly 'Chokepoint Data Pack' sold on Gumroad at around $12: the raw series behind every chart in the episode as CSV plus ready-made chart templates, Gatun Lake daily level, ACP daily transits and draft limits, auction clearing prices, and the Suez and Hormuz equivalents, each row carrying its source URL. A data-explainer audience is analysts, logistics staff and students who already rebuild these charts by hand, so the pack sells the thing the video's credibility advertises, and it can earn from episode one, years before the 1,000 subscribers and 4,000 watch hours AdSense requires. Free sample series pinned in the comments as the funnel.

competition_density 0.75 - the topic itself is crowded by entrenched incumbents (ten channels above, five of them over 490,000 views on this exact subject) and new entrants are publishing it weekly, which is why this is high rather than moderate. It is not 1.0 because none of them has the angle: every one of the ten frames it as drought plus queue plus the Rio Indio fix, and none prices the water. The topic title also collides directly with Wendover's 'The World's Shortcut', which is a reason to differentiate hard in packaging.

angle, water per transit - WaterWorld ('Leveraging data to optimize shipping through the Panama Canal while protecting local water supply') and Adimar Shipping's 2026 operational guide: a Panamax transit spends roughly 50-52 million US gallons of fresh water, about 197,000 cubic metres, while Neo-Panamax locks reclaim about 60 percent via the water-saving basins. Same sources: Gatun Lake supplies the locks and the drinking water for more than 50 percent of Panama's population.

angle, the auction price - Splash247 'Panama Canal slot auctions hit record $4m', Maritime Executive 'Panama Canal Auction Sets Record $4M for Slot as Congestion Grows', and gCaptain's reporting on surging bids: slots that cleared at roughly $135,000-$140,000 before the Strait of Hormuz conflict rose to $385,000-$425,000 average premiums by April-May 2026, then to a $4.6m bid by SK Shipping's LPG carrier G. Arete and a record $5.3m the following week, surpassing the late-2023 drought peak. That price series is the episode's main chart.

angle, the comparison figure - Wikipedia 'Water supply and sanitation in Panama', citing World Bank data: the average urban water and sanitation tariff in Panama City was $0.26 per cubic metre. The figure is from 2012 and will be captioned with its year and its age on screen rather than presented as current, and the on-screen ratio will be given as an order of magnitude, not a decimal.

angle, Rio Indio - Panama Canal Authority (pancanal.com, 'Rio Indio Lake Project Established as a Top Priority for National Water Security'), gCaptain and FreightWaves: the ACP approved the $1.6 billion Rio Indio reservoir in February 2025, damming the Indio River and driving a five-mile transfer tunnel to Gatun Lake, to secure water for more than half of Panama's population and allow up to roughly 15 extra transits per day. Construction is expected to start in 2027 and run five to six years, so nothing is stored before about 2032.

angle, the scarcity is structural not a one-off - Panama Canal Authority FY2024 figures reported by Woodwell Climate and the US Bureau of Transportation Statistics: daily transits fell from 36-38 in July 2023 to about 18-22 per day by February 2024, Gatun Lake stood almost 6 feet below its prior-year level on 1 January 2024 and lower than any January on record, and FY2024 closed at 9,936 transits against 12,638 in FY2023, a 29 percent fall. Munoz et al., 'Drying of the Panama Canal in a Warming Climate', Geophysical Research Letters (2025), finds that under high-emissions pathways the drought conditions that currently curtail transits become commonplace by the end of the century. Rainfall across the watershed from May to August 2026 ran about 34 percent below the long-term average even after the recovery.

affiliate_angle - the pack's contents are all series this episode already has to assemble from public sources (ACP daily transit and draft notices at pancanal.com, EIA chokepoint tonnage at eia.gov, Copernicus Sentinel lake-extent imagery, the auction clearing prices reported by Splash247 and Maritime Executive), so the marginal cost of packaging it is near zero and the sourcing is already done for the video.
